statement: In a given circle to inscribe a fifteen-angled figure which shall be both equilateral and equiangular.
heath_proof: Let ABCD be the given circle; thus it is required to inscribe in the circle ABCD a fifteenangled figure which shall be both equilateral and equiangular. In the circle ABCD let there be inscribed a side AC of the equilateral triangle inscribed in it, and a side AB of an equilateral pentagon; therefore, of the equal segments of which there are fifteen in the circle ABCD, there will be five in the circumference ABC which is one-third of the circle, and there will be three in the circumference AB which is one-fifth of the circle; therefore in the remainder BC there will be two of the equal segments. Let BC be bisected at E; [III. 30] therefore each of the circumferences BE, EC is a fifteenth of the circle ABCD. If therefore we join BE, EC and fit into the circle ABCD straight lines equal to them and in contiguity, a fifteen-angled figure which is both equilateral and equiangular will have been inscribed in it.
ai_proof_text:
4.16
**Statement:** In a given circle to inscribe a fifteen-angled figure which shall be both equilateral and equiangular.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be the given circle. Construct an equilateral triangle LMN (1.1). Since LM = LN, the angles at M and N are equal, and since ML = MN, the angles at L and N are equal (1.5); hence the three angles of the triangle LMN are equal to one another (CN1).

**Step 2.** In the circle ABCD inscribe a triangle ACK equiangular with the triangle LMN, taking A as one of its vertices (4.2). The three angles of ACK are respectively equal to the three angles of LMN, and these are equal to one another; therefore the angles CAK, ACK, AKC are equal to one another (CN1).

**Step 3.** The angle AKC at the circumference stands upon the arc AC, the angle CAK upon the arc CK, and the angle ACK upon the arc KA. Since these angles are equal, the arcs upon which they stand are equal (3.26): arc AC = arc CK = arc KA. These three arcs together make up the whole circumference of the circle.

**Step 4.** In the same circle inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon ABFGH having A as a vertex (4.11), its vertices lying in the order A, B, F, G, H round the circle, and let B be that vertex adjacent to A for which the arc AB proceeds from A along the circumference in the same direction as the arc AC. Since the chords AB, BF, FG, GH, HA are equal, the arcs between adjacent vertices which they cut off are equal (3.28): arc AB = arc BF = arc FG = arc GH = arc HA. These five arcs together make up the whole circumference.

**Step 5.** The arc AB is less than the arc AC. For otherwise each of the five equal arcs AB, BF, FG, GH, HA would be not less than AC, so that the five together would be not less than five arcs each equal to AC; but five arcs each equal to AC are greater than three such arcs (CN5), that is, greater than the whole circumference (Step 3); thus the five arcs AB, BF, FG, GH, HA would exceed the whole circumference, which is impossible, since they make up exactly that circumference. Therefore, the arcs AB and AC proceeding from A in the same direction, the point B lies on the arc AC, and the arc AC is made up of the arcs AB and BC.

**Step 6.** Bisect the arc BC at the point E (3.30), so that arc BE = arc EC. Then the arc AC is made up of the arc AB together with two arcs each equal to BE (CN2).

**Step 7.** Three arcs each equal to AC make up the whole circumference (Step 3), and five arcs each equal to AB make up the whole circumference (Step 4); therefore three arcs each equal to AC are equal to five arcs each equal to AB (CN1). By Step 6, three arcs each equal to AC are made up of three arcs each equal to AB together with six arcs each equal to BE (CN2). Hence three arcs each equal to AB together with six arcs each equal to BE are equal to five arcs each equal to AB; and, taking away three arcs each equal to AB from both, six arcs each equal to BE are equal to two arcs each equal to AB (CN3).

**Step 8.** Therefore three arcs each equal to BE are equal to the arc AB. For if three arcs each equal to BE were greater than AB, then six arcs each equal to BE, being made up of two such sets of three, would contain two arcs each equal to AB together with a surplus, and so would be greater than two arcs each equal to AB (CN5), contrary to Step 7; and if three arcs each equal to BE were less than AB, then in the same way two arcs each equal to AB would be greater than six arcs each equal to BE (CN5), again contrary to Step 7.

**Step 9.** Consequently the arc AC, being made up of AB and two arcs each equal to BE (Step 6), is equal to five arcs each equal to BE (CN2); and the whole circumference, being made up of five arcs each equal to AB (Step 4), is equal to fifteen arcs each equal to BE (CN2).

**Step 10.** Since arc BE = arc EC, the chords BE and EC are equal (3.29). The chord BE, being a straight line in the circle, is not greater than the diameter (3.15); so, proceeding from C along the circumference in the same direction (away from E), fit into the circle successively the chords CP₁, P₁P₂, P₂P₃, …, P₁₁P₁₂, each equal to the chord BE (4.1). Each of these chords cuts off an arc equal to the arc BE (3.28). Thus the fourteen consecutive arcs BE, EC, CP₁, P₁P₂, …, P₁₁P₁₂ are each equal to the arc BE.

**Step 11.** Fourteen arcs each equal to BE are less than fifteen such arcs (CN5), that is, less than the whole circumference (Step 9); hence these fourteen consecutive arcs, beginning at B, do not reach round to B, and there remains the arc P₁₂B which together with them makes up the whole circumference. Taking the fourteen arcs from the whole circumference, which is fifteen arcs each equal to BE, the remaining arc P₁₂B is equal to the arc BE (CN3). Therefore the chord P₁₂B is equal to the chord BE (3.29).

**Step 12.** Thus the fifteen-sided figure BECP₁P₂…P₁₂ has its fifteen sides BE, EC, CP₁, P₁P₂, …, P₁₁P₁₂, P₁₂B each equal to BE, and therefore equal to one another (CN1): the figure is equilateral. Each of its angles lies on the circumference of the circle ABCD, so the figure is inscribed in the circle (D4.3).

**Step 13.** Again, each angle of the figure stands upon the arc of the circle remote from its vertex, cut off by the two sides containing it; thus the angle BEC at E stands upon the arc CP₁P₂…P₁₂B, which is made up of the thirteen arcs CP₁, P₁P₂, …, P₁₁P₁₂, P₁₂B, each equal to BE. In the same way each of the fifteen angles stands upon an arc made up of thirteen of the fifteen equal arcs; these arcs are therefore equal to one another (CN2), and the angles at the circumference standing upon them are equal (3.27). Therefore the figure is equiangular.

**Step 14.** Therefore in the given circle ABCD a fifteen-angled figure which is both equilateral and equiangular has been inscribed. Q.E.F.

Path note: the equal arcs of the inscribed triangle were obtained directly from its equal angles by 3.26 (rather than via 1.6 and 3.28), and the inscribed equilateral triangle was obtained by 1.1 with 4.2 (rather than from alternate vertices of the hexagon of 4.15), these being the most direct routes.
